editorial.headline: Motor-Rider Gear Retail: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity covers essential rider equipment, from helmets and rainwear to gloves and masks—nationally open to full foreign ownership, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
PMA registration for this activity is not available to foreigners in Bali today. The activity is the retail sale of motor-vehicle rider equipment: helmets, jackets, raincoats, gloves and masks, offered through direct sales as well. It is a practical retail category built around the things riders wear for protection and comfort on the road—not the vehicles themselves, but the equipment that accompanies their use.

The registration scope is broad in business scale. It is open to micro, small, medium and large enterprises, allowing the activity to sit within anything from a modest specialist shop to a larger retail operation. That breadth matters because the commercial character remains the same across the scales: the business is retailing rider gear named within the activity’s scope. The record does not add separate operational requirements or carve-outs, so the useful reading is a disciplined one: register only for the retail activity described, at a scale the business genuinely occupies.

At the national level, the PMA position is clear. The activity is open, and foreign ownership may reach 100%. In ordinary terms, there is no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. That national openness is grounded in the cited PMA source, but it should not be mistaken for a guarantee of registrability in every location.

Bali is the decisive exception. For PMA registration, the activity is blocked under Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. The record identifies the relevant risk position at large scale as low or medium-low across every scope, which places the activity within that moratorium. The result is straightforward: full foreign ownership is nationally permitted, yet a PMA company cannot register this activity in Bali under the stated provincial rule. Founders considering Bali should treat that as the controlling present-tense fact, rather than relying solely on the national ownership ceiling.
